--- title: "Multiple linear regression" subtitle: "Types of predictors" date: "September 10, 2026" author: Shane Rybacki date-format: "MMMM DD, YYYY" footer: "[🔗 sta221-fa26.github.io](https://sta221-fa26.github.io)" logo: "../images/logo.png" format: revealjs: theme: slides.scss multiplex: false transition: fade slide-number: true incremental: false chalkboard: true include-before: [ ''] html: output-file: 06-predictor-type-notes.html html-math-method: method: mathjax url: "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjax@3/es5/tex-mml-chtml.js" execute: freeze: auto echo: true knitr: opts_chunk: R.options: width: 200 bibliography: references.bib --- ## Announcements - HW 01 due **TODAY** at 11:59pm - Ishrit's office hours today 1:15 - 4pm (see Canvas for location) - Professor Tackett's office hours canceled today ## Who is this Shane guy? {.midi} - 2nd year PhD student in Statistical Science - From San Antonio, Texas - Undergrad from the University of Texas at Austin (Hook 'em 🤘) - Degrees in Math and Business - Worked in consulting for a year (where I made PowerPoints for a living) before starting PhD ::::: {style="display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; gap: 6rem;"} ::: {} ::: ::: {} ::: ::::: ## Topics - Categorical predictors - Centering quantitative predictors - Standardizing quantitative predictors ## Computing setup ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # load packages library(tidyverse) library(tidymodels) library(openintro) library(patchwork) library(knitr) library(kableExtra) library(viridis) #adjust color palette # set default theme and larger font size for ggplot2 ggplot2::theme_set(ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 16)) ``` ::: ## Data: Lemurs ::: {.cell} ::: ::: midi Today’s data contains a subset of the original Duke Lemur data set available in the [TidyTuesday GitHub repo](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/blob/master/data/2021/2021-08-24/readme.md). This data includes information on 252 lemurs less than 24 months old from three taxa: - Eulemur rufus (ERUF), commonly known as Red-fronted brown lemur - Propithecus coquereli (PCOQ), commonly known as Coquerel’s sifaka - Varecia rubra (VRUB), commonly known as Red ruffed lemur. ::: :::::: columns ::: {.column width="33%"} ![ERUF](images/06-eruf-lemur.jpg){fig-align="center"} ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} ![PCOQ](images/06-pcoq-lemur.jpg){fig-align="center"} ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} ![VRUB](images/06-vrub-lemur.png){fig-align="center"} ::: :::::: ::: small Images from [Duke Lemur Center - Meet the Lemurs](Duke%20Lemur%20Center.%20n.d.%20“Meet%20the%20Lemurs.”%20https://lemur.duke.edu/discover/meet-the-lemurs/) ::: ## Variables **Predictors**: - `taxon` : Code made as a combination of the lemur’s genus and species. Note that the genus is a broader categorization that includes lemurs from multiple species. (`ERUF`: Eulemur rufus, `PCOQ`: Propithecus coquereli, `VRUB`: Varecia rubra) - `age`: Age of the lemur when weight was recorded (in months) - `litter_size`: Total number of infants in the litter the lemur was born into (this includes the observed lemur) **Response**: `weight`: Weight of the lemur (in grams) ## Response vs. predictors ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06-predictor-types_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: . . . **Goal**: Use age, taxon, and litter size to understand variability in the weight of lemurs younger than 24 months old. ## Model fit in R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lemur_fit <- lm(weight ~ age + taxon + litter_size, data = lemurs) tidy(lemur_fit) |> kable(digits = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:-----------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | -0.772| 116.993| -0.007| 0.995| |age | 137.479| 4.845| 28.377| 0.000| |taxonPCOQ | 462.184| 95.287| 4.850| 0.000| |taxonVRUB | 1020.390| 133.468| 7.645| 0.000| |litter_size | -14.101| 65.756| -0.214| 0.830| ::: ::: # Categorical predictors ## Matrix form of multiple linear regression $$\underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} y_1 \\ \vdots \\ y_n \end{bmatrix} }_ {\mathbf{y}} \hspace{3mm} = \hspace{3mm} \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 &x_{11} & \dots & x_{1p}\\ \vdots & \vdots &\ddots & \vdots \\ 1 & x_{n1} & \dots &x_{np} \end{bmatrix} }_{\mathbf{X}} \hspace{2mm} \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \beta_0 \\ \beta_1 \\ \vdots \\ \beta_p \end{bmatrix} }_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \hspace{3mm} + \hspace{3mm} \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \epsilon_1 \\ \vdots\\ \epsilon_n \end{bmatrix} }_\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$$
How might we include a categorical predictor with $k$ levels in the design matrix, $\mathbf{X}$ ?
## Indicator variables - Suppose there is a categorical variable with $k$ levels - We can make $k$ indicator variables from the data - one indicator for each level - An **indicator variable** takes values 1 or 0 - 1 if the observation belongs to that level - 0 if the observation does not belong to that level ## Indicator variables {.midi} Suppose we want to predict the amount of sleep a Duke student gets based on whether they are in Pratt (Pratt Yes/ No are the only two options). Consider the model $$Sleep_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1\mathbf{1}(Pratt_i = \texttt{Yes}) + \beta_2\mathbf{1}(Pratt_i = \texttt{No})$$ ::: question - Write out the design matrix for this hypothesized linear model. - Demonstrate that the design matrix is not of full column rank (that is, affirmatively provide one of the columns in terms of the others). - Use this intuition to explain why when we include categorical predictors, we cannot include both indicators for every level of the variable *and* an intercept. ::: ## Indicator variables for `taxon` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} lemurs <- lemurs |> mutate( eruf = factor(if_else(taxon == "ERUF", 1, 0)), pcoq = factor(if_else(taxon == "PCOQ", 1, 0)), vrub = factor(if_else(taxon == "VRUB", 1, 0)) ) ``` ::: . . . ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 4 taxon eruf pcoq vrub 1 ERUF 1 0 0 2 PCOQ 0 1 0 3 VRUB 0 0 1 ``` ::: ::: ## Trying to use all indicators in R {.midi} ::: question Run the code below to fit a model using `age`, `litter_size`, and all the indicator variables for `taxon` to predict `weight`. What do you notice about the model output? Why did this happen? ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lm(weight ~ age + eruf + pcoq + vrub + litter_size, data = lemurs) |> tidy() |> kable(digits = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:-----------|---------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 1019.618| 186.778| 5.459| 0.00| |age | 137.479| 4.845| 28.377| 0.00| |eruf1 | -1020.390| 133.468| -7.645| 0.00| |pcoq1 | -558.206| 129.187| -4.321| 0.00| |vrub1 | NA| NA| NA| NA| |litter_size | -14.101| 65.756| -0.214| 0.83| ::: ::: ## Indicator variables in the model {.midi} Given a categorical predictor with $k$ levels... - Use $k-1$ indicator variables in the model - The **baseline** is the category that doesn't have a term in the model - This is also called the *reference level* - The coefficients of the indicator variables in the model are interpreted as the expected change in the response compared to the baseline, holding all other variables constant. ## AE: Model in R {.midi} ::: question Now let’s take a look at the first five rows of the design matrix for the model with predictors `age`, `taxon`, and `litter_size`. How does R choose the baseline level by default? ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} model.matrix(weight ~ age + taxon + litter_size, data = lemurs)[1:5,] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) age taxonPCOQ taxonVRUB litter_size 1 1 2.27 0 0 1 2 1 0.72 0 0 1 3 1 0.69 1 0 1 4 1 1.05 1 0 1 5 1 2.66 1 0 1 ``` ::: ::: ## Exploring indicator variables {.small} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
term estimate std.error statistic p.value
(Intercept) -0.772 116.993 -0.007 0.995
age 137.479 4.845 28.377 0.000
taxonPCOQ 462.184 95.287 4.850 0.000
taxonVRUB 1020.390 133.468 7.645 0.000
litter_size -14.101 65.756 -0.214 0.830
````` ::: ::: ::: question What is the intercept for lemurs from the - ERUF taxon? - PCOQ taxon? - VRUB taxon? ::: ## Interpreting `taxon` {.small} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
term estimate std.error statistic p.value
(Intercept) -0.772 116.993 -0.007 0.995
age 137.479 4.845 28.377 0.000
taxonPCOQ 462.184 95.287 4.850 0.000
taxonVRUB 1020.390 133.468 7.645 0.000
litter_size -14.101 65.756 -0.214 0.830
````` ::: ::: . . . ::: incremental - The baseline level is `ERUF`. - Lemurs from the PCOQ taxon weight about 462.184 grams more, on average, than lemurs from the ERUF taxon, holding age and litter size constant. ::: ## Centering - Centering a quantitative predictor means shifting every value by some constant $C$ - One common type of centering is **mean-centering**, in which every value of a predictor is shifted by its mean - Only quantitative predictors are centered - Can be helpful to center all quantitative predictors in the model for ease of interpretation ::: question What is one reason we might want to center quantitative predictors? What are the units of centered variables? ::: ## Centering {.midi} Use the `scale()` function with `center = TRUE` and `scale = FALSE` to mean-center variables ::: {.cell output-location='fragment'} ```{.r .cell-code} lemurs <- lemurs |> mutate(age_cent = scale(age, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE) ) lm(weight ~ age_cent + taxon + litter_size, data = lemurs) |> tidy() |> kable(digits = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:-----------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 1243.384| 106.760| 11.647| 0.00| |age_cent | 137.479| 4.845| 28.377| 0.00| |taxonPCOQ | 462.184| 95.287| 4.850| 0.00| |taxonVRUB | 1020.390| 133.468| 7.645| 0.00| |litter_size | -14.101| 65.756| -0.214| 0.83| ::: ::: ## Centering ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Term | Original Model| Centered Model| |:-----------|--------------:|--------------:| |(Intercept) | -0.772| 1243.384| |age | 137.479| 137.479| |taxonPCOQ | 462.184| 462.184| |taxonVRUB | 1020.390| 1020.390| |litter_size | -14.101| -14.101| ::: ::: ::: question How has the model changed? How has the model remained the same? ::: ## Is the intercept meaningful? ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:-----------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 1243.384| 106.760| 11.647| 0.00| |age_cent | 137.479| 4.845| 28.377| 0.00| |taxonPCOQ | 462.184| 95.287| 4.850| 0.00| |taxonVRUB | 1020.390| 133.468| 7.645| 0.00| |litter_size | -14.101| 65.756| -0.214| 0.83| ::: ::: ::: question Explain why the interpretation is still not meaningful? How can we use centering to address this? ::: ## Standardizing - Standardizing a quantitative predictor mean shifting every value by the mean and dividing by the standard deviation of that variable - Only quantitative predictors are standardized - Standardize all quantitative predictors in the model for ease of interpretation ::: question What is one reason we might want to standardize the quantitative predictors? What are the units of standardized variables? ::: ## Standardizing {.midi} Use the `scale()` function with `center = TRUE` and `scale = TRUE` to standardized variables ::: {.cell output-location='fragment'} ```{.r .cell-code} lemurs <- lemurs |> mutate(age_std = scale(age, center = TRUE, scale = TRUE), litter_size_std = scale(litter_size, center = TRUE, scale = TRUE)) lm(weight ~ age_std + taxon + litter_size_std, data = lemurs) |> tidy() |> kable(digits = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:---------------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 1219.100| 86.497| 14.094| 0.00| |age_std | 964.181| 33.977| 28.377| 0.00| |taxonPCOQ | 462.184| 95.287| 4.850| 0.00| |taxonVRUB | 1020.390| 133.468| 7.645| 0.00| |litter_size_std | -13.037| 60.795| -0.214| 0.83| ::: ::: ## Standardizing ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Term | Original Model| Standardized Model| |:-----------|--------------:|------------------:| |(Intercept) | -0.772| 1219.100| |age | 137.479| 964.181| |taxonPCOQ | 462.184| 462.184| |taxonVRUB | 1020.390| 1020.390| |litter_size | -14.101| -13.037| ::: ::: ::: question How has the model changed? How has the model remained the same? ::: ## Recap - Interpreted categorical predictors - Explored why the model includes $k-1$ terms for a categorical predictor with $k$ levels - Fit and interpreted models with centered and standardized variables ## Before next class - Complete [Lecture 07 prepare](../prepare/prepare-lec07.html) - Submit HW 01 due TODAY at 11:59pm

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
